documents.abstract: Distribution system load restoration is a sequential decision-making problem in which restoration actions must maximize served load, prioritize critical loads, and preserve power-flow feasibility. This paper proposes an explainable agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework for distribution system load restoration. The proposed framework uses multiple large language model (LLM) agents for planner guidance, strategic plan generation, decision arbitration, memory-based feedback, and explanation generation. Unlike unconstrained LLM-based control, the proposed method restricts agent decisions to feasible restoration actions and evaluates all candidate plans using deterministic AC power-flow feasibility checks. The framework is evaluated on IEEE 33-bus and 69-bus distribution feeders, as well as a larger IEEE 118-bus test case, and compared against reinforcement learning and planning baselines. The results show that the proposed agentic framework achieves better restoration performance while producing structured explanations for operator-facing decision support. A direct comparison with a Single-LLM-Agent baseline further shows that the proposed multi-agent decomposition improves weighted restored load and critical-load recovery compared with a monolithic LLM decision structure.

In high-rise fire emergencies, ascending firefighters must enter the staircase while occupants are still descending—a structurally unavoidable form of bidirectional flow. Counterflow is recognized as a contributor to staircase congestion, but its building-wide propagation has not been quantified from field data. This observational field study analyzes video counts from a full-building evacuation drill at a 22-story office building (≈2,400 participants); the drill was conducted as a phased evacuation, which serves as the observational context. The analysis focuses on a counterflow event during the normal flow period—after phase-related merging had concluded—isolating counterflow effects from merging. A single pedestrian ascending from Floor 1 to Floor 2 was followed by flow disruption across 14 floors (M2–14F); the stop wave satisfying the ≥ 3-s criterion spanned 12 floors (3F–14F). Congestion duration increased with floor height, from 10 s at Floor 3 to a maximum of 38 s at Floor 13, whereas peak density showed no floor-level trend but was uniformly elevated across affected floors, from a normal-flow mean of 1.36 p/m 2 to a congested mean of 2.18 p/m 2 . The apparent congestion front speed over Floors 3–14 was 0.861 m/s, with onset time increasing almost linearly with path distance, indicating a single coherent front; the resolution front advanced at 0.734 m/s, about 15 % more slowly. These findings provide field-based evidence of the floor-by-floor amplification of congestion duration and motivate—as a safety hypothesis requiring further validation—counterflow-aware evacuation planning where firefighter ascent may coincide with occupant descent.

Many machine learning (ML) models still operate as “black boxes”, limiting users’ ability to understand and trust automated decisions. While Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has advanced, most approaches emphasize model mechanisms or explanation strategies, paying little attention to how the structure of the data itself shapes explanation quality. In this work, we explore the role of locality in shaping the perceived explanation quality for Automatic Text Classification (ATC), where locality consists of how instances are positioned relative to neighbors in representation space. We propose a data-centric framework that characterizes locality using two structural factors: (i) the average similarity between an instance and its neighbors and (ii) the entropy of the local class distribution. Based on these factors, we generate explanations grounded in neighborhood structure through locality-based word clouds and compare them to attention-based explanations. Unlike prior work that typically assumes locality inherently improves explainability, our framework systematically investigates explainability as a function of the spatial organization of data representations , while also establishing a principled way to relate local data characteristics to human-perceived explanatory quality. A user study with over 40 participants across two datasets evaluates explanations under criteria of Satisfaction, Completeness, and Trust . Results reveal that instances in highly homogeneous regions (high similarity, low entropy) produce explanations that users consistently rate as clearer and more useful, with statistically significant differences across datasets. These findings highlight the importance of locality as a key factor in explainability, offering insights for the design of explanation strategies in ATC and broader XAI research.
